title: Where it's followed
hook: Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia, South Asia

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Yusuf and al-Shaybani, and your line: students carry it. Did you thank someone who learned from you, and what did they say back? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

On the wall of some mosques, and in some prayer apps, the afternoon prayer has two start times. Asr, standard. Asr, Hanafi. The Hanafi one comes later. Same sun, same city, same day. The difference is a shadow. In the Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali books, the afternoon prayer begins when an object's shadow grows as long as the object. The Hanafi school, following Abu Hanifa's view, waits until the shadow is twice as long. So a timetable printed for a city with Hanafi and non-Hanafi Muslims prints both, and each person knows which line is theirs. That second line is a small map. It tells you the school traveled. Today: where it's followed.
screen: `TWO TIMES FOR ONE PRAYER.` → `ONE SHADOW, OR TWO.` → `A TIMETABLE THAT IS A MAP.`

segments.voice: Start with the word for a school: madhhab, a way, a path someone takes. The Hanafi way left Kufa early. Yesterday's student, Abu Yusuf, sat as a judge for the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad, and judges trained in the school's books went out with the courts. Next, the empires that carried it. The Ottomans made the Hanafi school the law of their courts, from Istanbul out across Anatolia and the Balkans. So today a Muslim in Sarajevo or Skopje or Istanbul is often praying the way the Hanafi books describe. In Central Asia, in cities like Bukhara and Samarkand, Hanafi scholars wrote major works of the school. In South Asia, the Mughal court commissioned a large collection of Hanafi rulings known as the Fatawa 'Alamgiri. That's one reason the school is followed in Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. Then the line in today's index: the most followed school. Some writers describe it that way, pointing to the size of the regions it covers. There's no precise count of who follows which school, and some Muslims simply pray the way their parents and their local mosque do, without naming a madhhab at all. Last, what a map doesn't show. In each of those places, Hanafi Muslims live beside Shafi'is, Malikis, Hanbalis and Ja'fari Shia, sometimes in the same mosque. Hence two lines for Asr on one wall. Each school is a way someone goes, and the ways cross.
screen: `MADHHAB: A WAY SOMEONE TAKES.` · `CARRIED BY COURTS AND EMPIRES.` · `ISTANBUL, BUKHARA, LAHORE, DHAKA.` · `THE WAYS CROSS IN ONE MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: The practice: find it on a map. If you have one nearby, use it. If not, draw it in your mind. Start in Kufa, in Iraq. Move west to Istanbul, and north into the Balkans, to Sarajevo. Come back east, across the Caspian, to Bukhara and Samarkand. Then south, over the mountains, into Afghanistan, down to Lahore, across to Delhi and on to Dhaka. Picture one person in each city standing up for the afternoon prayer, a little later than their neighbor. Then let the map go and just breathe. If you pray, you can remember Muslims in one of those cities by name. The bell holds the time.
Where it's followed. The Hanafi school runs through Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia and South Asia, carried by its judges and by empires that made it the law of their courts. Today's word.
Your line: the most followed school. Today, if you meet someone from one of those places, ask which way their family prays, and listen for the answer. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Hanafi Muslims across Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia and South Asia follow the school's rulings on prayer, fasting and family law, and prayer timetables in mixed cities may list a separate Hanafi time for the afternoon prayer.

fork.setup: your prayer app shows two times for the afternoon prayer, a standard one and a later Hanafi one. why?
options: the schools measure the start by different shadow lengths.
fork.reveal: same prayer, same sun. the other Sunni schools start Asr when a shadow equals the object; the Hanafi school waits until it is twice as long.

original.note: Arabic: a way that someone goes; in law, a school such as the Hanafi school.

trapdoor: what you thought: the schools are separate sects in separate places.
what it means: they're ways of reading the law, and they cross in one city, even one mosque.
what a scholar hears: the Hanafi school as the court school of the Abbasid judges, the Ottomans and the Mughals, from Istanbul to Bukhara to Delhi.

sources.ref: Hanafi and majority positions on the start of Asr (shadow twice vs. equal to the object's length)

notes: The carry ('the most followed school') is a superlative fixed by the index; the teach frames it as how the school is usually described and says no precise count exists. Keeper may wish to soften the index carry.

Hanafi Asr (shadow twice the object's length, beyond the noon shadow) vs. the majority view (equal length): confirm; also confirm that timetables listing a separate Hanafi Asr are common enough to say 'some mosques and some prayer apps'.
Ottoman courts applying Hanafi law; Abbasid judges trained in the school: confirm framing.
'Central Asian Hanafi scholars wrote major works of the school' (e.g. al-Hidayah by al-Marghinani of Farghana): confirm.
Fatawa 'Alamgiri as a Mughal-commissioned Hanafi collection: confirm. Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Afghanistan named as largely Hanafi regions; Shia and other Sunni communities also live there.
Madhhab glossed as 'a way that someone goes' (root dh-h-b, to go): confirm.
